units.text: Dental pulp is the soft connective tissue inside a tooth. It contains the tooth's blood vessels, nerves and lymphatic supply. Think of it as the living tissue at the centre of the tooth, rather than the hard outer covering.

The periodontal ligament is connective tissue that joins cementum on the root to the surrounding alveolar bone. Its collagen attachments, called Sharpey's fibres, extend into both tissues. It also contains blood vessels and different kinds of cells.

Cementum is a thin covering over the root dentin. Cells called cementoblasts deposit its matrix. It has no blood vessels of its own. Cellular cementum contains cells called cementocytes; acellular cementum does not contain cementocytes.

Junctional epithelium is the specialised non-keratinised lining that attaches the gum tissue to the tooth. It uses attachments called hemidesmosomes. White blood cells can pass through this lining into the gingival sulcus, which is the space beside the tooth. This permeability is relevant to the local immune response and periodontal infection.

Salivary glands make saliva, which keeps the mouth moist and helps with chewing, speech and swallowing. The major glands are the parotid, submandibular and sublingual glands, and there are many smaller glands throughout the mouth.

Amelogenesis means making enamel. Cells called ameloblasts lay down an enamel matrix that contains proteins and water and becomes mineralised. Enamel proteins include amelogenins and enamelins. Enamel and bone differ: enamel matrix contains very little or no collagen.

H&E staining helps us see tissue structure under the microscope. Haematoxylin highlights nuclei and other basophilic structures in blue-purple. Eosin highlights cytoplasm and extracellular matrix proteins in pink. Stain appearance can vary between laboratories and preparation runs.

Immunohistochemistry uses the specific interaction between an antibody and its antigen to highlight particular proteins in tissue. A chromogenic substrate makes the interaction visible; DAB produces a brown precipitate. This explains the staining principle rather than interpreting a patient's result.

Fixation preserves tissue by stopping autolysis and degradation and stabilising its structure and molecular components. Formaldehyde forms cross-links among proteins. Both too little and too much fixation can complicate later analysis, including immunohistochemistry.

Tissue processing prepares a specimen for thin sections. Processing removes water and allows paraffin wax to infiltrate the tissue. The tissue is then embedded in a wax block, which helps it stay firm during cutting. The orientation chosen during embedding determines the plane seen on the slide.

[Research context: 2017; retrospective patient series; human. 276 Brazilian patients with oral candidiasis. Limitations: Retrospective selected cohort; findings do not generalize to all populations or determine individual treatment. Educational research evidence; not a clinical recommendation. Faculty review pending.]

Oral candidiasis is a fungal infection in the mouth caused by Candida yeasts. Candida can live as a commensal, but conditions that favour its growth can allow it to cause disease. This patient series does not determine an individual treatment.

A normal distribution is a continuous bell-shaped distribution, also called a Gaussian distribution. It is described by its mean and standard deviation. The mean locates its centre, while the standard deviation describes its spread. A normal curve is a model; it does not mean that every measurement follows that model.

A frequentist 95% confidence interval describes a procedure that would include the fixed population value in about 95% of intervals if the study were repeated under its assumptions. It does not mean there is a 95% probability that the fixed population mean lies inside one particular calculated interval.
The arithmetic mean is the familiar average: add the observed values and divide by the number of observations. It summarises a set of measurements with one number.

One-way analysis of variance, or ANOVA, can compare the population means of several groups. The null hypothesis says the group means are all equal. The alternative says at least one differs; it does not identify which groups differ by itself.
